Photograph: PR Venice film festival French thriller Jupiter brings nuclear anxiety to red carpets of Venice Director Alexandre Smia says film about Russia detonating nuclear warhead – and US refusing to respond – is not unrealistic Philip Oltermann in Venice Sun 6 Sep 2026 06.37 EDT Last modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 07.07 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google R ussia has detonated a nuclear warhead over the Black Sea to underline its desire to revenge an assassination attempt on the Russian president. Germany and Italy urge restraint. The American president opts out of the standoff altogether and moots taking out Ukraine’s leader to appease Moscow. A new thriller, which has brought nuclear anxiety to the red carpets of the Venice film festival this week, plays through what would happen next. In Jupiter, which premiered on the Lido on Friday, the duty to square up to the Kremlin and enter the stress-inducing mind games of the nuclear deterrent falls on the fictional French president Paul Archambault (played by the hulking French actor Denis Ménochet), who is backed in his mission by the British prime minister. View image in fullscreen Denis Ménochet plays a fictional French president in Alexandre Smia’s film. Photograph: PR It’s a scenario that is far from unrealistic, the French film-maker Alexandre Smia said on the eve of his film’s premiere. “Even if the US disengagement from Nato is not official, we have reason to doubt that the US would offer its nuclear umbrella if one European city were to be attacked nowadays,” said Smia, who has previously directed episodes of the French spy TV series Le Bureau des Légendes. “And considering that France is the only country in Europe that is both a member of the European community, of the security council of the United Nations and of Nato, it naturally becomes actually the country where the responsibility of making decisions lies.” He added: “Filling the void when faced by a threat is not even a choice any more, it becomes almost an obligation.” Scheduled for release in France in November, Jupiter will focus minds but also divide opinion before presidential elections next April. After the release of a trailer, some voices on the far right have tried to dismiss the production as a “propaganda film” intended to shore up support for a centrist candidate against Marine Le Pen’s National Rally. The film’s title, however, is far from a straightforward reference to the outgoing president Emmanuel Macron, who famously called for a “Jupiterian” head of state. François Mitterrand, too, was nicknamed Jupiter by the national press and the command room inside the bunker beneath the Palais d’Élysée, where most of the film’s action takes place, was named after the Roman king of the gods under Valéry Giscard d’Estaing. In the film, the French head of state, Archambault, enters the nuclear standoff still reeling from the loss of his daughter – a biographical note that evokes Charles de Gaulle (who lost a daughter to pneumonia) and Jacques Chirac (who outlived his daughter Laurence). skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to The Guide Get our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every Friday after newsletter promotion EU’s ability to defend against invasion remains in doubt, finds official report Read more The socialist ex-president Hollande advised the makers of the film during their research, and Smia said he had picked Ménochet for the role precisely because he did not physically resemble any previous president. Yet while Jupiter is unequivocal about the need for French leadership, the film does not necessarily show that France is up to the job. To be taken seriously by the film’s Putin-equivalent character, its French president is forced to engage with Richard Nixon’s madman theory: giving off an appearance of irrationality to make otherwise non-credible threats seem credible. It’s a move that risks incensing the French public and alienating the president’s political allies in Europe and within his own cabinet. “Would any European leader be able to play the madman?” asked Smia. “The theory of the madman is indeed dangerous and I don’t think that any European leader would do that.” Lead actor Ménochet, who previously played a French president in Guy Maddin’s oddball G7 comedy Rumours, is best known to cinema lovers as a French farmer who crumbles under the interrogation of Christoph Waltz’s Nazi general in the opening scene of Quentin Tarantino’s Inglourious Basterds. View image in fullscreen Ménochet was cast in the film partly because he does not resemble previous French presidents. Photograph: PR In Jupiter, his character must display the utmost mental robustness, especially in the face of personal insults by the film’s Russian president Chernov, who implies that Archambault’s daughter lost her life because of western “decadence”. At screenings on the Lido, French journalists left the auditorium fiercely debating whether the film was an advert for a more aggressive French stance or a warning against it. The sustained ambiguity of Smia’s film puts it in a line with a number of recent works of French cinema that are set in contained spaces, prioritise verbal sparring over plot twists and leave audiences debating moral rights and wrongs, such as courtroom dramas Anatomy of a Fall by Justine Triet and The Goldman Case by Cédric Kahn, who also plays a supporting role in Jupiter. “This trend is very important and I hope it will become a movement,” said Smia. “In a time of simplification, films about moral ambiguities, about the difficulty of finding your own path and direction, are very, very important.” Explore more on these topics Venice film festival France Europe Nato features Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Robert Pattinson says he had ‘twice as much time’ after birth of first child Jim Jarmusch’s Father Mother Sister Brother, starring Cate Blanchett, surprise winner of Venice Golden Lion The Voice of Hind Rajab gets 23-minute ovation at Venice film festival Activists hope to shift Venice film festival focus on to crisis in Gaza Almodóvar’s The Room Next Door wins Golden Lion at Venice film festival ‘Like criticising a book that has 700 pages’: The Brutalist director defends long films Nicole Kidman’s erotic drama Babygirl sets pulses racing at Venice film festival Angelina Jolie says women are defined too much by other people’s perceptions Cate Blanchett says there is a ‘distinct lack of shame’ in modern society Separated review – Errol Morris’s quietly furious takedown of Trump’s inhumane border policy Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.dw.com/en/sudan-drone-strike.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OTvP Medical workers, including from Medecins Sans Frontieres, worked to treat the wounded at the nearby Ameth Bek hospital Image: Medecins Sans Frontieres/REUTERS Advertisement A drone strike in a busy market in the disputed region of Abyei has killed more than 150 people, according to local officials. South Sudanese officials blamed Sudan 's military for the attack, without providing evidence, amid the long-running civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia, which is reportedly active in the Abyei area. The special UN mission in Abyei warned in May that the RSF's presence in the resource-rich region had put residents in additional danger, and risked intensifying the older territorial dispute between Sudan and the world's newest sovereign state, South Sudan . Satellite images gave a sense of the scale of the damage after the large fire triggered by the drone strikes Image: Planet Labs PBC/REUTERS What do we know about the drone strike? According to local authorities, the attack hit the busy Amiet Market at around midday on Monday. Yohana Akol Ngor, the caretaker information minister in Abyei, told Reuters news agency on Tuesday that the death toll had more than doubled, reaching at least 153 compared to a stated figure of 73 the previous day. He said that Sudan's military was responsible for the attack but did not provide evidence. Akol Ngor said around 8,000 people had been displaced by the bombing. South Sudan's Foreign Ministry also blamed the Sudanese army and said the drone struck multiple locations around the busy market. One of these, judging by witness accounts, was a fuel depot — and this led to a large fire that proved difficult to bring under control overnight and was still ablaze on Tuesday. South Sudan said it had summoned Sudan's ambassador to protest and urged Sudan to "refrain from any actions that endanger civilian lives and property." Medical charity Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF), or Doctors Without Borders, said that its staff was treating some 20 wounded people at the nearby Ameth Bek hospital. "So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted," said Dr. Christian Lindauer, MSF's medical activities manager at the hospital. Many of the wounded were taken to Ameth Bek hospital for treatment Image: Medecins Sans Frontieres/REUTERS What's the backstory of Sudan, South Sudan and Abyei? The oil-rich Abyei region's status was not resolved by the 2005 peace agreement that broadly ended decades of civil war in Sudan. It was also not settled in 2011 when South Sudan became an independent country. A referendum was planned but never materialized, stalling over disputes on who should be allowed to vote. This left Abyei in a state of limbo, jointly administered and with an interim UN security force on site for 15 years. The region's majority Ngok Dinka population favors joining South Sudan, while Misseriya nomads who use its pastures favor Sudan. Amiet Market, the site of the attack, is an important trading hub for both communities. The unstable region has also experienced intercommunal violence in recent years between Ngok Dinka and neighboring Twic Dinka communities and is home to other armed militias. Medecins Sans Frontieres said its staff were providing surgical services, wound dressing and other emergency care to more than 20 wounded Image: Medecins Sans Frontieres/REUTERS How does this fit into Sudan's army's war with the RSF? The April 2023 outbreak of fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary — which has turned into a conflict with fairly entrenched battle lines, putting Sudan into a de facto state of partition — is increasing tension in the already-strained region. Abyei borders South Kordofan state in Sudan, which has become a major center of fighting in the war. Sudan's military alleges that the RSF is also operating out of Abyei. The United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) issued a similar statement in May. Officials in Abyei and South Sudan dispute this, however. Sudan's military and the RSF have both been using drones extensively in the conflict . "We remain alarmed by the relentless drone attacks across Sudan, as well as the damage they are causing to critical infrastructure — these attacks are taking a devastating toll on communities already struggling with the consequences of more than three years of conflict," UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric told reporters in New York on Tuesday when asked about the attack.
